isolation: Disconnecting equipment from every source of supply so it cannot be switched back on by accident. Normally done with an isolator that can be locked off.
lock-off: Fitting your own padlock (and a tag) to an isolator in the off position, so nobody else can switch it on while you work.
voltage indicator: A two-pole tester made for proving circuits dead. It shows if voltage is present between its two probes.
proving unit: A small battery-powered device that produces a test voltage, used to check a voltage indicator works before and after use.
prove-test-prove: Prove the tester works, test the circuit, then prove the tester again. Only then can the test result be trusted.
GS38: HSE guidance on electrical test equipment for low voltage systems. It covers safe probes, leads and how testers are used.
permit to work: A formal written system for controlling high-risk work. It lists hazards, isolations, precautions and who may work, and is issued and cancelled formally.
arc flash: An explosive release of energy when current flows through the air between conductors. It causes burns, blast and molten metal spray.
hazardous area: A place where flammable gas, vapour or dust can form an explosive atmosphere. Divided into zones. Only certified "Ex" equipment may be used.
DOL: Direct-on-line: a motor is switched straight onto the full supply voltage.
FLC: Full-load current: the current a motor draws at its rated output. Shown on the nameplate.
MPCB: Motor protection circuit breaker. Switches and protects a motor circuit. In this course it is used for short-circuit protection.
contactor: An electrically operated switch. When its coil is energised, its main poles and auxiliary contacts change over.
overload relay: A device that measures motor current and trips if it stays too high for too long, protecting the motor from overheating.
NO: Normally open: a contact that is open at rest and closes when operated.
NC: Normally closed: a contact that is closed at rest and opens when operated.
holding contact: An auxiliary NO contact of the contactor wired across the START button, keeping the coil energised after START is released. Also called a latch or retaining contact.
nameplate: The plate on a motor giving its rated voltage(s) and connection, current, power, speed, power factor and frequency. Read it before connecting or setting protection.
star: Star (Y) connection: one end of each winding is joined at a common star point. Each winding gets the line voltage ÷ √3 (230 V on a 400 V supply).
delta: Delta (Δ) connection: the windings are joined end to end in a ring, and each winding sits across two lines, getting the full line voltage (400 V).
insulation resistance: The resistance between conductors and earth (or between conductors), measured in megohms with an insulation tester at a high DC test voltage. Low values mean damaged or damp insulation.
interlock: An arrangement that stops two things happening together, such as two contactors closing at once. Electrical interlocks use NC contacts; mechanical interlocks use a physical lever.
phase sequence: The order in which the three phases reach their peaks (L1, L2, L3). It sets the direction of a three-phase motor; swapping any two phases reverses it.
on-delay timer: A timing relay whose contacts change over a set time after its coil is energised, and change back as soon as the coil is de-energised.
soft starter: A starter that uses thyristors to raise the motor voltage gradually, limiting starting current and torque. It does not change speed once started and is not an isolator.
thyristor: A semiconductor switch for AC power. Once triggered it conducts until the current falls to zero, so a soft starter can control voltage by choosing when in each half-cycle to trigger it.
